Why did you make this website?

I made this website because I knew Oakland's trash bills were expensive, but I wanted to quantify how expensive.

A major contributor to illegal dumping in Oakland is high rates and small trash containers, as noted by the 2025–2026 Alameda County Grand Jury Final Report.

That report also calls out the very high expense of trash disposal at the Davis Street Transfer Station in San Leandro, which is the closest place to dispose of trash for much of East Oakland.

And not all illegal dumping in Oakland is done by residents. With lax enforcement and high trash rates across the region, the city is seen as a dumping ground by neighboring cities.

Get involved in ending illegal dumping in the Bay Area

Oakland's contract with Waste Management runs from 2015 to 2030. Now is the time to get involved to bring down East Bay trash bills and end illegal dumping systemically.

Volunteer your free time to clean illegal dumping sites and that does make an immediate difference, but the ultimate long-term solution is to make simple changes to public policy.

Illegal dumping in Oakland is a multi-faceted issue. Here are some ideas to end it:

  1. Separate Oakland into multiple waste collection zones
    High-cost-to-service areas such as the Oakland Hills, with their narrow and hilly streets are currently being subsidized by the easy-to-service areas of the Oakland Flats because both currently pay exactly the same rate.

    By introducing separate waste collection zones, service providers can more accurately price their services based on the actual cost to provide the service to a given area. The service providers don't even need to be the same. Each waste collection zone can be competed for and operated independently by different providers.
  2. Be a public observer in city contract negotiations
    Trash haulers have been accused of illegally colluding and bribing elected officials, including the ongoing federal corruption case involving former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao. A bad 15-year contract is effectively a sentence on an entire generation of people to grow up in an environment with illegal dumping.

    The city's previous "requests for proposal" for trash hauling in 2015 inexplicably ended up with a single provider bidding. It's vital this does not happen again.

    It's too important to rely on city workers and elected officials to get this right without help. Public observation throughout the entire process will help ensure integrity and maintain an impartial, competitive bidding process.
  3. Require more than one bulky-waste pickup a year
    Currently, apartment buildings and multi-family homes only get a single free bulky-waste pickup despite an apartment building potentially holding hundreds of households.

    In order to end dumping of bulky furniture, every unit in a multi-family home and apartment building must have one free disposal of bulky waste included in its service.
  4. Be civically engaged: attend city council meetings and your local neighborhood association, and make your representatives aware of the sheer expense of Oakland's current trash rates by regional standards. Lowest-income ZIP codes are hit hardest, and they're also where illegal dumping is most concentrated.
  5. Consider a bounty system that pays modest amounts for recorded video that leads to prosecution for illegal dumping, to change the culture of silent acceptance. A “snitches get riches” policy could start as a small-scale private philanthropic effort.
    This will work best after solving the underlying issues around disposal costs.

Remember: This is not just an Oakland problem. People from outside Oakland have been caught renting U-Hauls to dump within Oakland. We need to work together to address the cost of waste management in neighboring cities, certainly including San Pablo, Orinda and Piedmont. Their high rates hurt the region.
